title: Large sums on lines called "other"
question: How much of an organization's spending, assets or change in worth sits on catch-all lines, and what does the return say those sums are?
finding: 132 organizations have at least one catch-all line that is large for their size: 44 with "other changes in net assets" of $100,000 or more and a tenth of expenses, 28 with a prior-period adjustment of that size, 10 with undescribed "all other expenses" above 10% of spending, 33 with one self-described other expense above 40% of spending, 20 with "other fees for services" above half, and 28 with "other assets" of $1 million or more that are over half of everything they own. 38 of the 163 rows carry no description the script could find; the largest of those is a prior-period adjustment of $81.4 million at Yerba Buena Center For The Arts in the year ended 30 June 2025, against $11.6 million of expenses.
how: From each full return: other changes in net assets and prior-period adjustments (Part XI lines 9 and 8), all other expenses (Part IX line 24e), the largest expense the organization itself added and named (lines 24a to 24d), other fees for services (line 11g), and other assets (Part X line 15). Each is compared with total expenses, or with total assets for the last. The description is the return's own wording, cut to twelve words: the label typed on the line, the first matching note in the return's explanations schedule, or the items listed for other assets. For each organization and line the year with the largest share is shown. Rows with no description come first, then the rest, each by share; the share is held at 100% where the line is as large as its base.
limits: These lines exist to be used, and most of what is on them is routine: a pass-through agency reports the money it passes on as an "other" expense, a housing developer holds partnership interests as "other assets", an accounting-standard change runs through "other changes in net assets". The form asks for an explanation when such lines are large, and many returns give one; where the description column is empty the explanation may still be there under a heading this script did not recognise. Rounding and preparer habits weigh heavily here. A large unexplained line is a question for the audited statements and their notes. A pattern here is a reason to ask for the audited statements, not a finding.
